Mechanism of action

Ondansetron work by antagonizing the serotonin 5 HT3 receptors centrally and peripherally

Centrally it antagonizes the 5HT 3 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (normally neurotransmitters like serotonin, toxins and other signals play a role in mediating nausea and vomiting by activating this zone); so by antagonizing serotonin 5HT 3 receptors there, ondansetron work to suppress nausea and vomiting

Ondansetron also work peripherally by antagonizing the serotonin 5HT 3 receptors in the vagus nerve terminals; vagus nerve can sense nausea and vomiting triggers in the GI tract and delivering sensations to nucleus tractus solitarius in the brainstem (another region important in vomiting), so by blocking vagus nerve sensation, nausea and vomiting are suppressed

Most of ondansetron antiemetic effect is coming from the peripheral 5HT 3 receptor antagonism with a minor contribution coming from the central antagonism

Therapeutic uses

FDA approved therapeutic uses:

Prevention of chemotherapy induced nausea and vomiting (first line)

Treatment of Radiation induced nausea and vomiting (first line)

Prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting (first line)

Off label use:

Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with pregnancy, According to ACOG, pyridoxine alone or combined with doxylamine is the preferred pharmacological therapy for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy but in refractory cases, ondansetron 4 mg orally every 8 hours maybe considered; ondansetron is pregnancy category B medication

Acute treatment of cyclic vomiting syndrome

For treatment of severe refractory diarrhea associated with neuroendocrine tumors (carcinoid syndrome)

In treatment of nausea and vomiting associated with gastroenteritis

In treatment of irritable bowel syndrome

Pharmacokinetics

Ondansetron is available as oral, IM, and IV formulations

Oral formula is rapidly absorbed from the GI tract, with 60% bioavailability

It is metabolized by CYP enzymes in the liver and excreted through kidney with a half life around 4 hours

Adverse effects

Most commonly side effects include headaches, fatigue, dry mouth, malaise, diarrhea and constipation

Less common side effects include drowsiness, sedation, local injection site reactions and pruritus

Ondansetron may lead to a hepatocellular pattern of elevation in liver enzymes and rare cases of acute liver injury

Ondansetron may lead to ECG changes such as QT interval prolongation => this may lead to torsade de pointes arrhythmias and other types of arrhythmias; IV administration has a higher risk for causing these effects; FDA does not recommend a single dose higher than 16 mg IV to prevent those effects

There is reported cases of bradycardia and asystole with this medication

Ondansetron impair gut motility to some degree that why there is reported cases of intestinal obstruction (rare)

It may also lead to SJS in some patients

Drug- Drug interactions

Concurrent administration with pimozide with ondansetron should be avoided because both lead to QT interval prolongation, amiodarone and other torsadogenic drugs may do the same

Ondansetron may lead to serotonin syndrome if co administered with other serotonergic medications

Contraindications

Previous hypersensitivity reactions to the drug

ondansetron is contraindicated in patients on apomorphine => this can lead to profound hypotension and loss of consciousness with ondansetron enhancing the hypotensive effect of apomorphine

Monitoring

Electrolytes and ECG monitoring are suggested in patients treated with ondansetron who have high risk for arrhythmia; such as family history of prolonged QT interval, heart failure, electrolyte disturbance
